1 Kaplan-Meier

The Kaplan–Meier estimator, also known as the product limit estimator, is a non-parametric statistic used to estimate the survival function from lifetime data.

library(survival)
data(cancer, package="survival")

veteran -> df

df$trt <- factor(df$trt,
                 levels = c(1, 2),
                 labels = c("standard", "test"))

head(df)
       trt celltype time status karno diagtime age prior
1 standard squamous   72      1    60        7  69     0
2 standard squamous  411      1    70        5  64    10
3 standard squamous  228      1    60        3  38     0
4 standard squamous  126      1    60        9  63    10
5 standard squamous  118      1    70       11  65    10
6 standard squamous   10      1    20        5  49     0
fit_1 <- survfit(Surv(time, status == 1) ~ 1,
               data = df,
               stype=1, #kaplan-meier
               ctype = 1,
               conf.type = "log-log"
               )  

fit_1

2 AFT model

2.1 Log-Normal AFT model

2.1.1 Interpretation

(Dabney 2025) (phút 14:13)

(Sinha 2024) (trang 14)

\[Y_i = log(T_i) = \beta_0 + X_i^T \beta_1 + U_i\]

where \(U_i\) has a known distribution. This model is known as accelerated failure time (AFT) model.

If the distribution of \(U\) is assumed to be a known family of distributions, we call it parametric AFT otherwise it is a non-parametric AFT model.

A special case is when \(U_i\) is assumed to follow \(\texttt{Normal}(0, \sigma)\) distribution, then the distribution of \(T_i\) is called lognormal.

library(survival)
data(cancer, package="survival")

veteran$trt <- factor(veteran$trt, 
                      levels = c(1, 2), 
                      labels = c("standard", "test"))


mod_lnorm <- survreg(Surv(time, status == 1) ~ trt,
                     data = veteran, 
                     dist = "lognormal")

summary(mod_lnorm)

Call:
survreg(formula = Surv(time, status == 1) ~ trt, data = veteran, 
    dist = "lognormal")
              Value Std. Error     z       p
(Intercept)  4.2461     0.1677 25.31 < 2e-16
trttest     -0.1777     0.2375 -0.75    0.45
Log(scale)   0.3188     0.0628  5.08 3.9e-07

Scale= 1.38 

Log Normal distribution
Loglik(model)= -749.2   Loglik(intercept only)= -749.5
    Chisq= 0.56 on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.45 
Number of Newton-Raphson Iterations: 2 
n= 137

This implies an estimated mean log survival time of 4.2461 for the standard group; and an estimated mean log \(4.2461 + (- 0.177) = 4.0691\) for the test group.

p-value = 0.45 > 0.05 it indicates the treatment effect is not statistically significant.

Note

Biện luận cho biến liên tục, tham khảo (Breheny 2017) (trang 26)

Ví dụ biến stage có hệ số -0.4294, nghĩa là one-uit change in stage shorten survival time by 35%, vì \(e^{-0.4294} = 0.65\), do đó 1 - 0.65 = 0.35.

Ví dụ biến age có hệ số +0.4294, nghĩa là one-uit change in age increase lên survival time by 53.6%, vì \(e^{0.4294} = 1.536\), do đó 1.536 - 1 = 0.536.

  • 95%CI for \(\beta_1\) (coefficient for trt)

\[-0.1777 \pm 1.96 \times 0.2375 = [-0.643, 0.288]\]

beta1_est <- coef(mod_lnorm)["trttest"]

se_beta1 <- summary(mod_lnorm)$table["trttest", "Std. Error"]

ci_beta1 <- beta1_est + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se_beta1

ci_beta1
[1] -0.6431794  0.2877348
  • 95%CI for \(\sigma\) (scale parameter)

For the scale parameter \(\sigma\), we construct a CI on the log-scale:

\[log(1.3755) \pm 1.96 \times 0.0628 \Rightarrow \text{CI for log}(\sigma)=[0.196,0.441]\]

Exponentiating, we obtain the CI for \(\sigma\) is \([1.216, 1.556]\)

sigma_est <- mod_lnorm$scale

se_sigma <- summary(mod_lnorm)$table["Log(scale)", "Std. Error"]

log_sigma <- log(sigma_est)

ci_log_sigma <- log_sigma + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se_sigma

ci_sigma <- exp(ci_log_sigma)

ci_sigma
[1] 1.216172 1.555714
Note

Scale parameter \(\sigma\), which governs the variability of the log-survival times.

2.1.2 Prediction

Using the model-based survival function for the log-Normal AFT model, we compute the estimated survival probabilities at time = 100 for each treatment group.

  • For the standard group (trt = 1):

\[\hat{S}(100| \mathtt{standard}) = 1 - \Phi \bigg(\frac{log(100)- \beta_0}{ \sigma}\bigg) = 1 - \Phi \bigg(\frac{log(100)- 4.2461}{ 1.38 }\bigg) \approx 0.397\]

  • For the test group (trt = 2):

\[\hat{S}(100| \mathtt{test}) = 1 - \Phi \bigg(\frac{log(100)- (\beta_0 + \beta_1)}{ \sigma}\bigg) = 1 - \Phi \bigg(\frac{log(100) - (4.2461 + (-0.1777))}{ 1.38 }\bigg) \approx 0.348\]

beta0 <- coef(mod_lnorm)["(Intercept)"]

beta1 <- coef(mod_lnorm)["trttest"]

sigma_hat <- mod_lnorm$scale

# Compute survival probability at t = 100
t_star <- 100

# Standard treatment group (trt = "standard")
lp_standard <- beta0

S_standard <- 1 - pnorm( (log(t_star) - lp_standard) / sigma_hat)
S_standard
(Intercept) 
  0.3970241 
# Test treatment group (trt = "test")
lp_test <- beta0 + beta1

S_test <- 1 - pnorm((log(t_star) - lp_test) / sigma_hat)
S_test
(Intercept) 
  0.3481712

2.1.3 Plot

Plot the fitted survival curves (from the original model) for the two treatment groups on the same graph.

# Extract coefficients and scale
beta0 <- coef(mod_lnorm)["(Intercept)"]
beta1 <- coef(mod_lnorm)["trttest"]
sigma <- mod_lnorm$scale

# Define time grid for plotting
range(veteran$time)
[1]   1 999
t_grid <- seq(0,
              1000, 
              length.out = 300)

# Linear predictors for each group
lp_standard <- beta0
lp_test <- beta0 + beta1

# Survival function estimates for each group
S_standard <- 1 - pnorm((log(t_grid) - lp_standard) / sigma)

S_test <- 1 - pnorm((log(t_grid) - lp_test) / sigma)
plot(x = t_grid, 
     y = S_standard, 
     type = "l", 
     lwd = 2, 
     las = 1,
     col = "blue",
     ylim = c(0, 1), 
     xlab = "Time", 
     ylab = "Estimated Survival Probability",
     main = "Model-Based Survival Curves (log-Normal AFT)")

lines(x = t_grid, 
      y = S_test, 
      col = "red", 
      lwd = 2, 
      lty = 2)

legend("topright", 
       legend = c("Standard", "Test"),
       col = c("blue", "red"), 
       lwd = 2, 
       lty = c(1, 2))

abline(h = 0,
       col = "darkgreen")

abline(v = 0,
       col = "darkgreen")

We generated survival curves based on the log-Normal AFT model for both treatment groups over time. The plot above compares estimated survival probabilities for the standard and test groups.

The standard group shows slightly higher survival probabilities over time rather than test group, though the difference is modest and not statistically significant.

2.2 Exponential AFT model

2.2.1 Interpretation

\[Y_i = log(T_i) = \beta_0 + X_i^T \beta_1 + U_i\]

where random noise \(exp(U_i)\) follow the exponential distribution with mean \(\lambda_0\).

library(survival)
data(cancer, package="survival")

veteran$trt <- factor(veteran$trt, 
                      levels = c(1, 2), 
                      labels = c("standard", "test"))


mod_exp <- survreg(Surv(time, status == 1) ~ trt,
                     data = veteran, 
                     dist = "exponential")

summary(mod_exp)

Call:
survreg(formula = Surv(time, status == 1) ~ trt, data = veteran, 
    dist = "exponential")
             Value Std. Error     z      p
(Intercept) 4.8214     0.1250 38.57 <2e-16
trttest     0.0928     0.1768  0.53    0.6

Scale fixed at 1 

Exponential distribution
Loglik(model)= -751.1   Loglik(intercept only)= -751.2
    Chisq= 0.28 on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.6 
Number of Newton-Raphson Iterations: 5 
n= 137

The treatment coefficient is small (0.0928) and statistically nonsignificant (p-value = 0.6 < 0.05), indicating no evidence of a difference in survival times between the two treatment groups under the exponential AFT formulation.

2.2.2 Prediction

Using the model-based survival function for the exponential AFT model, we compute the estimated survival probabilities at time = 100 for each treatment group.

For the exponential AFT model, the survival functions is

\[S(t|x) = exp(-t \times exp(-\eta))\]

where \(\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\)

Using the estimated coefficients:

\(\hat{S}(100|\texttt{standard}) = exp(-100 \times exp(- 4.8214)) = 0.4468\)

\(\hat{S}(100|\texttt{test}) = exp(-100 \times exp(- 4.8214 - 0.0928)) = 0.4799\)

Both groups have survival probabilities at time 100 just below 0.50, with the test group slightly higher.

# Extract estimated coefficients
beta0_exp <- coef(mod_exp)["(Intercept)"]
beta1_exp <- coef(mod_exp)["trttest"]

# Compute linear predictor for each group
lp_standard <- beta0_exp # trt = "standard"
lp_test <- beta0_exp + beta1_exp # trt = "test"

# Compute survival probability at time = 100
t0 <- 100

S_standard <- exp( -t0 * exp(-lp_standard) )

S_standard
(Intercept) 
  0.4468474 
S_test <- exp( -t0 * exp(-lp_test) )

S_test
(Intercept) 
  0.4799308

Tính CI

# Covariance matrix of estimated coefficients
V <- vcov(mod_exp)
V
            (Intercept)   trttest
(Intercept)    0.015625 -0.015625
trttest       -0.015625  0.031250
# Estimated beta vector
beta_hat <- coef(mod_exp) # Named vector

# Define function to compute CI for S(t | x) (slides 25{26)
CI_S_exp <- function(x_star, t0 = 100, beta_hat, V) {
  
# a = (1, x*)
a <- c(1, x_star)
# Linear predictor
eta_hat <- sum(a * beta_hat)
# Variance of eta_hat = a^T V a
var_eta <- as.numeric(t(a) %*% V %*% a)
se_eta <- sqrt(var_eta)
# CI for eta
ci_eta <- eta_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se_eta
# CI for S(t | x) = exp( -t * exp(-eta) )
S_hat <- exp( -t0 * exp(-eta_hat) )
ci_S <- exp( -t0 * exp(-ci_eta) ) # Note: reversed direction due to exp(-eta)
return(list(S_hat = S_hat, CI = ci_S))

}
# Compute CIs

CI_standard <- CI_S_exp(x_star = 0, #trt = standard (ref level)
                        t0 = 100, 
                        b = beta_hat,
                        V = V)
CI_standard
$S_hat
[1] 0.4468474

$CI
[1] 0.3573025 0.5323265
CI_test <- CI_S_exp(x_star = 1, #trt = test
                    t0 = 100, 
                    b = beta_hat, 
                    V = V)
CI_test
$S_hat
[1] 0.4799308

$CI
[1] 0.3914416 0.5629335

2.2.3 Mean and median

# Design matrix rows for standard and test treatment groups
x_std <- c(1, 0) # intercept + trt = standard (ref level)

x_test <- c(1, 1) # intercept + trt = test

2.2.3.1 Mean

# Function to compute estimate and CI for mean survival time
mean_surv_ci <- function(x_vec, V, b) {
eta <- sum(x_vec * b)
se_eta <- drop(sqrt(t(x_vec) %*% V %*% x_vec))
ci_eta <- eta + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se_eta
est <- exp(eta)
ci <- exp(ci_eta)
return(list(estimate = est, CI = ci))
}
mean_std <- mean_surv_ci(x_std, V, beta_hat)
mean_std
$estimate
[1] 124.1406

$CI
[1]  97.16587 158.60399
mean_test <- mean_surv_ci(x_test, V, beta_hat)
mean_test
$estimate
[1] 136.2187

$CI
[1] 106.6195 174.0352

2.2.3.2 Median

# Function to compute estimate and CI for median survival time
median_surv_ci <- function(x_vec, V, b) {
eta <- sum(x_vec * b)
se_eta <- drop(sqrt(t(x_vec) %*% V %*% x_vec))
ci_eta <- eta + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se_eta
est <- log(2) * exp(eta)
ci <- log(2) * exp(ci_eta)
return(list(estimate = est, CI = ci))
}
median_std <- median_surv_ci(x_std, V, beta_hat)
median_std
$estimate
[1] 86.04772

$CI
[1]  67.35025 109.93591
median_test <- median_surv_ci(x_test, V, beta_hat)
median_test
$estimate
[1] 94.41964

$CI
[1]  73.90302 120.63200

2.3 Weibull AFT model

2.3.1 Interpretation

\[Y_i = log(T_i) = \beta_0 + X_i^T \beta_1 + U_i\]

where \(\epsilon_i = exp(U_i)\) follows the Weibull distribution with the scale \(b\) and shape \(a\).

library(survival)
data(cancer, package="survival")

veteran$trt <- factor(veteran$trt, 
                      levels = c(1, 2), 
                      labels = c("standard", "test"))


mod_weib <- survreg(Surv(time, status == 1) ~ trt,
                     data = veteran, 
                     dist = "weibull")

summary(mod_weib)

Call:
survreg(formula = Surv(time, status == 1) ~ trt, data = veteran, 
    dist = "weibull")
             Value Std. Error     z      p
(Intercept) 4.7697     0.1479 32.25 <2e-16
trttest     0.0478     0.2079  0.23  0.818
Log(scale)  0.1585     0.0673  2.35  0.019

Scale= 1.17 

Weibull distribution
Loglik(model)= -748.1   Loglik(intercept only)= -748.1
    Chisq= 0.05 on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 0.82 
Number of Newton-Raphson Iterations: 5 
n= 137

The estimated coefficient for trttest is 0.048, which is not statistically significant (p-value = 0.818).

The shape parameter (scale) estimate is 1.17, indicating modest deviation from the exponential distribution.

2.3.2 Prediction

# Extract estimated shape
ahat <- 1 / mod_weib$scale
# Extract coefficients
b0 <- mod_weib$coefficients[1]
b1 <- mod_weib$coefficients[2]
# Define covariates: x = 0 (control), x = 1 (treatment)
x_std <- 0
x_test <- 1
# Target time t
t0 <- 100
# Compute estimated survival probabilities at t = 100
S_std <- exp(- (t0 * exp(-b0 - x_std * b1))^ahat)
S_std
(Intercept) 
  0.4193591 
S_test <- exp(- (t0 * exp(-b0 - x_test * b1))^ahat)
S_test
(Intercept) 
  0.4341928

3 Cox PH model

library(survival)
sim_ph <- read.csv("HW_6_data_1.csv")

head(sim_ph)
       time status trt  age
1  6.689445      1   1 70.2
2  6.835349      1   0 41.5
3 32.835707      1   1 56.0
4  2.053170      1   0 47.2
5  8.651760      1   1 74.1
6  6.525246      1   1 75.7
# Convert treatment to factor (with meaningful labels)

sim_ph$trt <- factor(sim_ph$trt, 
                     levels = c(0, 1),
                     labels = c("Control", "Treatment"))

\[\lambda(t|X) = \lambda_0(t)exp(X' \beta)\]

\[log(\lambda(t|x_i)) = log(\lambda_0(t)) + \beta_1 trt_i + \beta_2 age_i\]

fit_1 <- coxph(Surv(time, status == 1) ~ trt + age,
               data = sim_ph)

summary(fit_1)
Call:
coxph(formula = Surv(time, status == 1) ~ trt + age, data = sim_ph)

  n= 200, number of events= 193 

                  coef exp(coef)  se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)    
trtTreatment -0.727337  0.483194  0.153839 -4.728 2.27e-06 ***
age           0.033869  1.034449  0.006292  5.383 7.33e-08 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

             exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
trtTreatment    0.4832     2.0696    0.3574    0.6532
age             1.0344     0.9667    1.0218    1.0473

Concordance= 0.649  (se = 0.022 )
Likelihood ratio test= 43.58  on 2 df,   p=3e-10
Wald test            = 43.15  on 2 df,   p=4e-10
Score (logrank) test = 44.29  on 2 df,   p=2e-10

The coefficient for trtTreatment is −0.727, corresponding to a hazard ratio of \(exp(−0.727) \approx 0.483\). This means that, holding age constant, participants in the Treatment group have about 48.3% the hazard of participants in the Control group; i.e., they are less likely to experience the event at any given time point. The effect is statistically significant.

Note

If trtTreatment is 0.727, corresponding to a hazard ratio of \(exp(0.727) \approx 2.06\). This means that: holding age constant, participants in the Treatment group have about 2.06 times the hazard of participants in the Control group; i.e., Treatment group are MUCH likely to experience the event at any given time point in comparison to Control group.

The coefficient for age is 0.0339, corresponding to a hazard ratio of \(exp(0.0339) \approx 1.034\). This implies that, holding trt group constant, each additional year of age is associated with a 1.034 - 1 = 0.034 = 3.4 % increase in the hazard of experiencing the event. The effect is statistically significant.

3.1 PH assumptions

3.1.1 Graphical approach

3.1.1.1 Biến phân loại

km_trt <- survfit(Surv(time, status == 1) ~ trt, 
                  data = sim_ph)

plot(km_trt, 
     fun = "cloglog", 
     col = c("blue", "red"), 
     lty = 1:2,
     xlab = "Time", 
     ylab = "log(-log(Survival))",
     main = "log(-log(S(t))) by Treatment Group")

legend("bottomright", 
       legend = levels(sim_ph$trt),
       col = c("blue", "red"), 
       lty = 1:2)

Since the two curves for trt appear approximately separated by a constant amount, the PH assumption appears (based on this graphical check) to be reasonable with respect to trt.

3.1.1.2 Biến liên tục

sim_ph$age_bin <- cut(sim_ph$age,
                      breaks = c(0, 50, 60, 70, 100),
                      include.lowest = FALSE,
                      right = TRUE,
                      labels = c("(0,50]",
                                 "(50,60]",
                                 "(60,70]", 
                                 "(70,100]")
                      )
km_age <- survfit(Surv(time, status == 1) ~ age_bin, 
                  data = sim_ph)

plot(km_age, 
     fun = "cloglog", 
     col = 1:4, 
     lty = 1:4,
     xlab = "Time", 
     ylab = "log(-log(Survival))",
     main = "log(-log(S(t))) by Age Group")

legend("bottomright",
       legend = levels(sim_ph$age_bin),
       col = 1:4, 
       lty = 1:4)

3.1.2 Hypothesis testing approach

H0: proportional hazards assumption is reasonable

H1: proportional hazards assumption is NOT hold

The p-value for trt is high, as expected, confirming our conclusion regarding the PH assumption with respect to trt.

The p-value for age is smaller but still reasonably high, supporting the PH assumption with respect to age.

cox.zph(fit_1)
         chisq df    p
trt    0.00126  1 0.97
age    1.56091  1 0.21
GLOBAL 1.59721  2 0.45

3.2 Baseline cumulative hazard

Baseline cumulative hazard function \(\Lambda_0(t)\)

basehaz_df <- basehaz(fit_1)
survfit_obj <- survfit(fit_1)

surv_df <- data.frame(
time = survfit_obj$time,
surv = survfit_obj$surv
)

surv_df$neglogsurv <- -log(surv_df$surv)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot() +
  
geom_step(data = basehaz_df, 
          aes(x = time, 
              y = hazard, 
              color = "basehaz()")) +
  
  geom_step(data = surv_df,
            aes(x = time, 
                y = neglogsurv, 
                color = "-log(S(t))")) +
  
  labs(title = "Baseline Cumulative Hazard Function Estimates",
       x = "Time",
       y = "Cumulative Hazard",
       color = "Method") +
theme_minimal()

3.3 Prediction

newdata_50 <- data.frame(
  trt = factor(c("Control", "Treatment")),
  age = c(50, 50)
)


fit_surv <- survfit(fit_1, 
                    newdata = newdata_50,
                    se.fit = F)

plot(fit_surv,
     col = c("blue", "red"),
     lty = 1:2,
     lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Time",
     ylab = "Survival Probability",
     main = "Cox PH survival curves by Treatment")

legend("bottomleft",
       legend = c("Control", "Treatment"),
       col = c("blue", "red"),
       lty = 1:2,
       lwd = 2)

The model-based survival curves suggest that survival prognosis (for a 50-year old) is better in the Treatment group than in the Control group.

3.4 Likelihood ratio test

fit_reduced <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ trt, data = sim_ph)

fit_full <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ trt * age, data = sim_ph)

# Likelihood ratio test comparing the two models
anova(fit_reduced, fit_full)
Analysis of Deviance Table
 Cox model: response is  Surv(time, status)
 Model 1: ~ trt
 Model 2: ~ trt * age
   loglik  Chisq Df Pr(>|Chi|)    
1 -820.80                         
2 -806.12 29.359  2  4.215e-07 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The LR test, based on 2 degrees of freedom, results in a test statistic value of 29.359 and a tiny p-value. This indicates that \(age\) and the \(trt \times age\) interaction terms contribute substantially to model fit quality.

3.5 Wald test

beta_hat <- coef(fit_full)

V <- vcov(fit_full)
# Define matrix A, compute Wald statistic and p-value.

A <- matrix(c(1, 0, 40,
              1, 0, 60),
            nrow = 2, 
            byrow = TRUE)

A_beta <- A %*% beta_hat

A_V_A_t <- A %*% V %*% t(A)

W <- t(A_beta) %*% solve(A_V_A_t) %*% A_beta

W
        [,1]
[1,] 23.0937
df <- nrow(A)

p_value <- pchisq(W, df = df, lower.tail = FALSE)

p_value
            [,1]
[1,] 9.66643e-06

\[log(\lambda(t|x_i)) = log(\lambda_0(t)) + \beta_1 trt_i + \beta_2 age_i + \beta_3(trt \times age)_i\]

\[\begin{array}{r} \text{Treatment effect for 40 years old: } \\ \text{log harzard: trt = 1, age = 40: constant} + \beta_1 + 40 \beta_2 + 40 \beta_3 \\ -\text{log harzard: trt = 0, age = 40: constant} ~~~~~~~~~+ 40 \beta_2~~~~~~~~~~~~~\\ \hline \color{Red}{1}\color{Black} \beta_1 +~~ \color{Red}{0} \color{Black}\beta_2 + \color{Red}{40} \color{Black} \beta_3 \end{array}\]

Giả thuyết:

\(H_0: A \beta = 0\) meaning Treatment effect at age 40 is NO effect. There is no different between Treatment and Control. In short, no treatment effect at age 40

\(H_1: A \beta \ne 0\) meaning Treatment effect at age 40 EXIST effect. There is different between Treatment and Control. In short, EXIST treatment effect at age 40.

Tương tự cho age 60.

The Wald test statistic equals 23.097, with 2 degrees of freedom, corresponding to a tiny p-value.

As a result, we reject the null hypothesis that there EXIST treatment effect at age 40 as well as 60.
